Imagine you are at a funeral, quietly mourning. Someone walks up to the grieving widow and says, "Well, at least now you can redecorate the house the way you always wanted!" The comment wasn't necessarily said out of cruelty — maybe the person was just trying to lighten the mood — but it was completely wrong for the moment. It didn't fit. It landed badly. It created awkwardness, maybe even hurt.

That comment was infelicitous.

Infelicitous means poorly suited, inappropriate, or badly chosen for the occasion or context — especially when it comes to words, remarks, or expressions. Something is infelicitous when it just doesn't fit where it was placed, when it creates an uncomfortable or jarring effect because someone chose the wrong thing to say (or do) at the wrong moment.

The word is most commonly used to describe:

1. Words and remarks. This is the most common use. An infelicitous remark is one where the speaker picked the wrong words, the wrong tone, or the wrong moment. It's a poor choice of expression. A politician who uses a joke about poverty while speaking to a homeless shelter audience has made an infelicitous remark. A manager who responds to an employee's resignation with "Finally, I was wondering how long you'd stick around!" has said something infelicitous.

2. Word choices in writing. In literary criticism, editors, critics, and professors use this word to describe writing where a word or phrase simply doesn't belong — where it jars the reader, sounds off, or feels wrong for the piece. A writer who uses cheerful, bouncy language in a chapter about grief has made infelicitous word choices.

3. Actions, decisions, and timing. Less commonly, but still correctly, you can call an action infelicitous when it is unsuitable for the circumstances. Throwing a wild party on the night your neighborhood is mourning a tragedy would be infelicitous behavior.
The Most Important Nuance: It's About Fit, Not Intent

This is crucial. Infelicitous does not mean:

  • Deliberately rude or cruel
  • Factually wrong
  • Morally bad

It means the wrong thing in the wrong place. The person may have had perfectly good intentions. They may have even been trying to help. But their choice — of words, action, or timing — simply did not suit the moment. It was a mismatch. A misfire.

Think of it like wearing a swimsuit to a job interview. You haven't done anything evil. You haven't lied. But it's the wrong choice for the context, and it creates a bad impression. That's the spirit of infelicitous.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Awkward is broader and more casual. Anything can be awkward — a silence, a stumble, a glance. Infelicitous is more specific: it's about something being poorly chosen or unsuited to the occasion.

Inappropriate is similar, but carries a stronger moral edge. Inappropriate can imply something is offensive or wrong in principle. Infelicitous is softer — it focuses on the mismatch between the expression and the context, not a moral failure.

Tactless focuses on a lack of sensitivity toward other people's feelings. Infelicitous focuses on the poor fit between the expression and the moment — the two often overlap, but they're not identical.

Clumsy or bungled describe execution. Infelicitous describes suitability. A brilliantly executed speech can still be infelicitous if it strikes the wrong note for the audience or occasion.

• The speaker's infelicitous comparison between the company's losses and a "minor inconvenience" angered many employees who had lost their jobs.
  • The editor flagged several infelicitous phrases in the manuscript where the author's tone shifted jarringly from solemn to playful.
  • It was an infelicitous moment to bring up salary negotiations — the team had just received news of layoffs.
  • His congratulatory email, sent to the wrong person, was not just embarrassing but deeply infelicitous given the circumstances.
  • The ambassador's infelicitous remarks about the host country's culture caused a minor diplomatic stir.
The Register of This Word — When Is It Used?

Infelicitous is a formal word. You will see and hear it in:

  • Literary criticism and book reviews
  • Journalism and political commentary
  • Academic writing
  • Careful, formal speech

You would not normally say to a friend, "That was infelicitous." You'd say, "That was a bit off," or "That was the wrong thing to say." But in formal writing or speech, infelicitous is the precise, elegant tool for the job.

Not all infelicitous things are equally bad. There is a spectrum:

At the mild end: a word that slightly jars in an essay. A slightly off-tone remark at a dinner party. A metaphor that doesn't quite land in a speech.

In the middle: a comment at a sensitive moment that causes real embarrassment or discomfort. A poorly chosen phrase in a public statement.

At the serious end: a remark so badly misjudged that it causes genuine offense, damages relationships, or creates a public scandal — even if no harm was intended.

The word covers this whole range, which is part of what makes it so useful.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Infelicitous = the wrong word, remark, or action for the moment — not necessarily evil, but badly misjudged, poorly suited, and landing in exactly the wrong way.
